questions.prompt: What does resistance do to electric current?
options: It slows and limits the flow
questions.explanation: Resistance is the drag that opposes the moving charge, limiting how much current flows.
questions.misconception: The direction is often flipped; resistance holds back, it never accelerates flow.

questions.prompt: In what unit is resistance measured?
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω); volts are the push, amps the flow.
questions.misconception: Ohm/volt/amp are the trio most often scrambled on labels and meters.

questions.prompt: With the same voltage, doubling the resistance does what to the current?
questions.explanation: current = voltage ÷ resistance; double the denominator and current halves.
questions.misconception: Some think resistance and current both rise together; they oppose each other.

questions.prompt: Which material offers almost no resistance to current?
questions.explanation: Metals like copper have tiny resistance; rubber and wood block current (insulators).
questions.misconception: Treating all materials equal; material is one of the two big deciding knobs of resistance.

questions.prompt: Compare two copper wires of the same material. Which has HIGHER resistance?
questions.explanation: Long thin paths fight the current most; short fat paths flow freely.
questions.misconception: The shape of the road matters as much as the material — both decide ohms.
